entries.title: Ancient Egyptian carvings like the Narmer Palette's long-necked beasts prove humans and dinosaurs coexisted
entries.summary: The intertwined-neck creatures on the 5,000-year-old Narmer Palette are a cataloged genre of Egyptian mythological beast, not a sauropod sighting, but the claim borrows credibility from a real, still-argued fight over what the Bible's Behemoth actually was.
entries.explain:
The Narmer Palette (c. 3100 BC) shows two long-necked animals on its reverse side with their necks crossed into a circle. Pseudoarchaeology sites call them dinosaurs; the correct term is serpopards: a serpent-necked, leopard-bodied composite creature that shows up repeatedly on other Egyptian cosmetic palettes and carved ivory wands from the same period. The necks bend in directions no sauropod spine could manage, and outside the neck, nothing about the animals' legs, tails, or heads resembles a real dinosaur. This is a known and recurring piece of Egyptian symbolic art, not an eyewitness sketch.

The claim persists because it's grafted onto a debate that is genuinely alive: what Job 40:15-24 means by "Behemoth." Answers in Genesis and the Institute for Creation Research argue in published, detailed articles that Behemoth is best read as a sauropod-type dinosaur, pointing to the tail "like a cedar" (Job 40:17), bones described as tubes of bronze and iron, its grass-eating diet, and its being called "the chief of the ways of God," which they take as the most impressive land animal God made. Notably, the major young-earth organizations do not cite the Narmer Palette or similar artifacts as part of that case; Creation Ministries International has run its own skeptical pieces on weak "dinosaur in ancient art" claims, meaning serious young-earth apologetics keeps some distance from this specific argument even while holding the sauropod reading of the text itself.

Mainstream Hebrew Bible scholarship answers the Behemoth question differently, and not with one voice. The traditional reading, going back through Jewish and patristic commentary, identifies Behemoth as a hippopotamus, a plant-eating, marsh-dwelling giant that fits verses about grazing "like an ox" and lying in the reeds. Michael Heiser argued a complementary but distinct point: that Behemoth, alongside Leviathan and Rahab, functioned in Hebrew poetry as a chaos-monster figure drawing on Canaanite and Ugaritic mythological language (the sea god Yam, the monster Tannin), used polemically to declare that Yahweh, not Baal or Marduk, is the one who subdues chaos. On that reading Job 40-41 is making a theological argument about God's power over the untamable, not a zoological field report.

So the honest verdict is layered. The Narmer Palette does not depict a dinosaur, full stop; that specific piece of "evidence" fails on the art itself. But it rides on a real disagreement between careful readers of Job, where young-earth and mainstream scholars cite different textual details for genuinely different conclusions. It deserved better than being cut as a baseless connection.

entries.title: A 12th-century carving at Ta Prohm temple near Angkor Wat shows a stegosaurus, proving dinosaurs survived into human history
entries.summary: The hand-sized carving at Ta Prohm reads as a plated dinosaur only if you crop out the matching leaf-motif backgrounds carved behind every other animal on the same wall.
entries.explain:
This carving rides the same underlying claim covered in the entry on Egyptian "dinosaur" art: that Job 40's Behemoth describes a literal dinosaur, and that physical artifacts should exist to back it up. Photographs of the small roundel carving at Ta Prohm (part of the Angkor temple complex built under Suryavarman VII in the late 1100s AD) began circulating among young-earth creationists including Don Patton in the mid-2000s, and Answers in Genesis ran a January 2007 piece treating it as evidence dinosaurs survived to historic times. Even Creation magazine, published by Creation Ministries International, ran its own back-page feature the same year raising the claim, then followed up more cautiously.

The carving doesn't strengthen that case even on its own terms. The same round, radiating background pattern appears carved behind other, unambiguous animals nearby on the same temple wall (a rhinoceros, water buffalo, and monkeys among them), which is the strongest evidence the "plates" are decorative foliage (stylized palm fronds or lotus leaves) rather than a spine of bony plates. A genuine stegosaur reconstruction also has paired, alternating plates and prominent tail spikes; this carving has neither. And even if it were a deliberate anachronism, it wouldn't actually move the debate: Stegosaurus dates to the Late Jurassic, roughly 150 million years before the Khmer Empire carved this wall, a gap so large that it dwarfs anything young-earth chronology needs: a framework that already allows for humans and dinosaurs overlapping by mere thousands of years, not tens of millions. Job 40-41 either supports that overlap on its own, or it doesn't; this carving can't add anything the text hasn't already claimed.

entries.title: Thousands of clay figurines dug up at Acámbaro, Mexico, include accurate dinosaur models too detailed for anyone who hadn't seen a living dinosaur
entries.summary: The figurines are a documented 1940s forgery ring, not a lost record of dinosaurs, but the claim keeps circulating because it's plugged into a real theological argument about Job's Behemoth.
entries.explain:
Waldemar Julsrud, a German-born merchant living in Acámbaro, Guanajuato, reported "discovering" the first of what grew into a collection of roughly 33,000 ceramic figurines starting in July 1944, many resembling dinosaurs, dragons, and other fantastical creatures. Archaeologist Charles C. DiPeso, working with the Amerind Foundation, investigated the site directly in 1952 and found the physical hallmarks of recent manufacture: no soil packed into surface crevices, no wear on broken edges, and no patina consistent with age. DiPeso also identified a local family who had been producing and selling the figurines to Julsrud for about a peso apiece since shortly after his "discovery," reportedly drawing inspiration from movies, comic books, and trips to Mexico City's national museum.

The dating history only reinforces the hoax finding. The University of Pennsylvania's MASCA lab ran thermoluminescence tests on a sample of the figurines between 1969 and 1972 and got dates around 2500 BC, a result authenticity advocates still quote. But follow-up analysis in 1978 showed the original method had failed to isolate true thermoluminescence and was instead reading chemiluminescence, an unrelated effect that mimics an old date; corrected readings point to manufacture in the late 1930s or early 1940s, right before the figurines surfaced. Even Answers in Genesis, a young-earth organization with every incentive to embrace physical evidence of human-dinosaur coexistence, has publicly treated the Acámbaro figurines as most likely fraudulent.

So why does this keep resurfacing in apologetics? Because it's serving a real argument, even if this particular artifact can't carry it. Young-earth readings of Job 40:15-24's Behemoth as a sauropod-type dinosaur (argued at length by Answers in Genesis, the Institute for Creation Research, and Genesis Apologetics) create a demand for physical corroboration that humans and dinosaurs once overlapped. Apologetics Press, a Church of Christ apologetics ministry, has published material defending the figurines as genuine for exactly this reason: because a text-only reading of Job can always be argued away, and a clay figurine feels like proof you can hold. The lesson isn't that the Behemoth question is fake; it's that a forged 1940s figurine can't settle it in either direction, and shouldn't be allowed to stand in for the real textual argument.

entries.title: The 'Baghdad Battery' (a roughly 2,000-year-old clay jar containing a copper cylinder and iron rod, found near Baghdad) was an ancient electrical battery, proof of lost advanced technology
entries.summary: The jar most likely held a decayed scroll, not a charge, and Genesis already makes a bolder, unremarked claim about early metalworking than "ancient people had a battery" ever could.
entries.explain:
German archaeologist Wilhelm König catalogued the object in the late 1930s: a ceramic jar holding a copper cylinder wrapped around an iron rod, sealed at the top with bitumen, found near Khujut Rabu outside Baghdad. König proposed in 1938 that it was a galvanic cell, possibly used to electroplate gold onto silver objects. The idea took off in popular culture, helped along by later demonstrations (including a MythBusters build) showing that a modern replica filled with an acidic liquid like vinegar or grape juice does generate a small voltage: a fact often mistaken for proof of the ancient object's actual purpose.

The archaeological case against the battery reading is straightforward. No wires, electrode arrays, or any device that could have used a current were ever found with the jars. No electroplated artifacts from the relevant period and region have been identified: the metal-gilding technique actually documented from Mesopotamia and Persia in this era is fire-and-mercury gilding, not electroplating. The jar's shape and construction match a known type of sealed storage vessel used for scrolls or other organic materials, which would explain both the metal components (a protective cylinder) and the acidic residue researchers have found inside (from decayed organic contents, not battery chemistry). Even the artifact's assumed date is disputed: König guessed Parthian (247 BC-224 AD), but its pottery style is a closer match for the later Sasanian period (224-651 AD).

What makes the "ancient tech shocks us" impulse worth engaging seriously is that Genesis already makes a much bigger and far less defensive claim about early technology, without any fanfare. Genesis 4:22 names Tubal-Cain (born just a handful of generations after Adam, and explicitly before the Flood) as "a forger of every cutting instrument of bronze and iron" (KJV; more literally, an instructor of craftsmen in both bronze and iron). The text treats sophisticated, specialized dual-metal smithing as ordinary background information in a genealogy, not a miracle needing explanation.

Real archaeology shows why this claim is more interesting than the battery ever was, rather than more embarrassing. Confirmed copper smelting goes back to roughly 5000 BC (the securely dated high-temperature smelting site at Belovode, Serbia, is the current oldest), with the broader Chalcolithic period running from about 4500-3300 BC across the Near East: genuine early metallurgy, well before most casual timelines assume. Iron is a later and rarer story: Dr. Naama Yahalom-Mack of the Hebrew University's Institute of Archaeology notes that iron remained a scarce, prestige metal through the twelfth and eleventh centuries BC, with over ninety percent of tools still made of bronze, and it didn't become the dominant utilitarian metal in the Levant until the tenth century BC. But isolated iron artifacts are much older than that industrial shift: Answers in Genesis's Philip Huber points to a worked iron bead from el-Gerzeh in Lower Egypt dated to the fourth millennium BC and a smelted iron dagger from Chagar Bazar in Syria, both real excavated finds rather than fringe claims. Mainstream archaeology reads these as rare, isolated early experiments (often using meteoric iron) long before industrial ironworking existed, not evidence of a lost pre-Flood civilization on the Genesis timeline, but both camps agree that skilled, specialized ancient metalworking reaches back further than casual assumption expects. That's exactly the point Genesis 4:22 is quietly making about Tubal-Cain, and it does it without any of the theatrics pseudo-archaeology piles onto artifacts like the Baghdad jar.

entries.title: Geologist Robert Schoch's water-erosion analysis shows the Great Sphinx is really 7,000 to 12,000 years old, thousands of years older than mainstream Egyptology allows
entries.summary: Schoch's rain-erosion case for a vastly older Sphinx has a serious mainstream rebuttal on the geology itself, and only one identifiable, narrow young-earth source engages the claim directly at all.
entries.explain:
Geologist Robert Schoch, of Boston University, argued starting in 1991 that the vertical, undulating weathering patterns on the walls enclosing the Great Sphinx look like the product of sustained rainfall rather than the wind-and-sand abrasion typical of Egypt's historical climate. Since Egypt hasn't seen rainfall on that scale since roughly 7000-5000 BC, Schoch concluded the Sphinx's core body must have been carved that far back, thousands of years before the conventional attribution to the pharaoh Khafre around 2500 BC.

The mainstream rebuttal, developed by geologist James Harrell (University of Toledo), Egyptologist Colin Reader, and Sphinx excavation director Mark Lehner, argues the same weathering pattern is fully explained by softer limestone layers eroding faster than harder ones under ordinary wind and occasional flash-flood runoff, compounded by the fact that the Sphinx spent most of its history buried in sand, which limits how much erosion time it actually accumulated. They also dispute Schoch's subsurface seismic readings as reflecting natural variation in the bedrock rather than a deeper weathering profile, and point to comparable weathering on securely dated Old Kingdom tombs cut from the same limestone. Michael Heiser reviewed this Reader-versus-Schoch exchange on his own site and came down on the side that a dramatically older Sphinx isn't required once burial history and limestone bedding are accounted for.

On how this intersects young-earth chronology and the post-Flood repopulation timeline specifically, the honest finding is that substantive engagement is thin. Searching the major young-earth organizations (Answers in Genesis, the Institute for Creation Research, Creation Ministries International) turns up no dedicated article taking on Schoch's redating claim directly; this is a case where the expected debate mostly isn't there in citable form. The one identifiable named source is narrower: the Northwest Creation Network's "Biblical Chronology" article (nwcreation.net, also mirrored on CreationWiki) proposes that a post-Flood ice age, within an Ussher-style young-earth timeline, overlapped early Egyptian history and ended roughly a century after Joseph, and suggests in passing that this wetter climate window "explains...the water erosion on The Great Sphinx," using it as circumstantial support for a compressed Egyptian chronology rather than adopting Schoch's actual multi-thousand-year redate, which would in fact be too old even for a young-earth Flood date typically placed around 2500-2350 BC. Beyond that one specific mention, there isn't a developed young-earth literature wrestling with Schoch's claim on its own terms: worth stating plainly rather than manufacturing a bigger fight than actually exists in print.
